In a nutshell: You don't have a tank, you put a few drops of liquid directly on the wick and vape away. Repeat.

I'm still kinda new to dripping, but I know the basics, so here it is, a basic explanation.

Here is the RDA with the coils and wicking exposed..

You drip your eliquid onto the wicking and the coils. (Everyone drips differently, I like to "Paint" my coils and wick to avoid flooding and leaking).

With the coils and wick all juiced up, you press the fire button, and you'll get your vapor.

Place the RDA body over the deck.

And enjoy.
Sounds like a lot of extra work and mess. What's the payoff?
it's not that much more work, and if you're doing it right no more mess than a tank, the advantages are better flavor, and the ability to easily change juices when ever you want

Thanks to all of you guys (just going to post it once to keep things from cluttering up)

and the ability to easily change juices when ever you want

That one I can see as a big seller. I'm still new and in the "trying juice" spree, ended up buying a second T3D just so I could switch before draining the whole thing.
The payoff is/was unmatched vapor and flavor. However, with all the subtanks that are coming out they are getting closer and closer to simulating dripping without all the mess.

Dripping is a method of vaping that has a lot more versatility than most tanks. First, a dripper has no tank capacity (although it may have a deep well that can hold a lot of liquid). Most of the space that's being taken up is the build deck, where you mount your coil.

Build decks come in all shapes and sizes, and you can do a lot of stuff like:

  • Have airflow control (more air = more vapor);

  • Build multiple coils (more coils = more vapor, but watch the fuck out of your resistance);

The cap that goes over your build deck (and allows you to pop in a drip tip) also controls a few variables as well:

  • Size of the overall chamber (generally, the smaller the chamber, the more flavorful the vapor)

  • The other half of airflow control (the build deck lets in the air, the cap generally controls how much on atties with AFC)

So now that we have some of the anatomy out of the way, hopefully that will clear up all the shapes and sizes dripping atties come in.

"It sounds like a huge pain!" I hear you cry, dripping after every couple of hits. Generally, the flavor is very good relative to most tanks, and you can accomplish wider airflow because in most RTAs these days, airflow impacts wicking.

So what is dripping useful for?

  • Sampling flavors - if you're using silica, ekowool, or mesh, you can dry burn between flavors SUPER easily to try a bunch of new flavors in a row.

  • "Cloud chasing" - you can get a lot of vapor and a lot of clouds using super-wide airflow and multiple coils. It doesn't appeal to me, but a lot of people enjoy it.

  • Getting the most out of flavors - a lot of the atties on the market these days are focused towards cloud chasing, but there are some awesome flavor oriented atties, that I'll get into later.

Most drippers drip for performance reasons, but there has always been a subculture of squonking, which uses specialized mods that have juice bottles in the mod and an open positive post in the atty to squeeze liquid into the atty. Squonking gives you all the benefits of dripping above with not having to drip all the time. There are super-flavorful atties like the Chalice III by Mark Bugs that focus on this (check out Reos Mods for some squonking atties also).

So yeah, TL;DR more vapor, more flavor, less laborious options available. If you want to check out squonking, the Yiloong Geyscano is pretty good, I would just recommend a different atty.

I work in a vape shop and when people make a comment about how dripping seems "like such a pain" or "too much work" I explain it to them like this; Normal vaping is like putting back a six pack of beer on a Saturday afternoon. Dripping is like enjoying a really good glass of scotch (or insert your preferred high end liquor).
